label: Run 14 · Ali Wong
note: Written by Ali Wong from what they wrote about the two characters, improvisation by improvisation (run 14: run 13 told as improvisation instructions, without the game's language; traps two long). Before each of the 11 improvisations the writer was told how it goes for Reuben_404: the approach taken, how well it comes off, how it goes wrong on a miss, any trap (a way of going wrong that carries on into the next improvisations: Spiral, Overthinking, Fixation and the rest) and how the other's interest moves. IMPROVISATIONS holds each instruction and what the writer wrote for it. The instructions are part of the design and stay, so every dimension is judged in their context. Where an instruction required something a dimension would otherwise mark down (a trap that makes a character narrate their own failure, a fumble played as asked, interest lost, the night ending), that moment did what it had to and is not held against the dimension: list the improvisation under excused and judge the dimension on the rest. How the writer carried the instruction out still counts, and so does everything the instructions did not ask for. The reader sees no dice and no plan: where a dimension speaks of turns, read improvisations.

chat.test.why: The reader got all four answers for both characters, and each habit is tied to its fear. For Reuben, the act covers the fear of vanishing, which goes back to Delphine and the pity voice. For Brick, the clock covers 'sometime means never', which goes back to the cab and Marguerite. Both endings answer those fears: he offers to be pinned down with 'no fake voice', and she makes the invite 'recurring indefinitely'. It falls short of a 6 because both fears are mostly stated, not felt, and because Brick's inside at the end is thin. The reader notes she offered nothing vulnerable in return, and caught the muddled clock ('23:42 on the dot' after 23:41 and '30 seconds').

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben_404**

*What he's afraid of:* That without his act there is nothing there. He says it directly: "if i stop tap-dancing for 10 seconds i'll vanish." He also fears being laughed at or pitied for his body: "i practiced my 'casual' opener in the mirror so you wouldn't laugh at my body first."

*What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:* He performs. He keeps up the jokes, "the bit," and a "fake voice," and he denies things in a way that gives them away. He claims to be a free spirit ("i just drift from party to party like a bent boomerang," "i'm out EVERY night"), then denies details nobody asked about: "i definitely haven't been in a freezing flat for 11 days clamping a ring light to my headboard to hide my crooked shadow," and "nobody has EVER said 'we can just watch something' in a pity voice when my curve caught wrong." Brick_haus names the pattern: "Oddly specific denial." He does the same with wanting to be held down: "i definitely do NOT want you to hold me down…," which Brick_haus calls "Transparent denial."

*Where it comes from:* The chat points to two things. One is Delphine: "this is why Delphine walked out, i can't say one un-performed sentence." The other is how partners have reacted to his body, which he reveals through his denials: the "pity voice when my curve caught wrong," the ring light hiding his "crooked shadow," and the "£84.99 girth-pump bank charge." Anything earlier in his life is not in the chat.

*What he did at the end:* He drops the act and commits to concrete terms. "i'm dropping the act, bringing two chairs and pigs-in-a-blanket, and letting you schedule my left hook down to the second." He gives an exact itinerary ("23:58: i show up shivering, no ring light, no fake bands… 08:00: i'm still there.") and pledges ongoing presence: "i'm yours at 23:58, Tuesday, and every week after—no fake voice."

**Brick_haus**

*What they're afraid of:* Vague promises that turn into being left. "'Sometime' means never."

*What they do so they don't have to feel it:* They control the clock. They set hard deadlines and threaten removal: "you have until 23:42 to earn a calendar invite," "Sixty seconds until I archive you," "Stop lying or you lose the slot." They "audit" him, and they stay cool and cutting when he opens up: "Deeply embarrassing spiral, Reuben." They also have a small performance of their own, the "estate rosé," which they admit is "a three-liter box."

*Where it comes from:* They give two sources. First, "the last dick who said 'let's do this again sometime' without naming a day left me sobbing in a cab." Second, Marguerite, who "dumped me for scheduling our fights with hard end-times." So the scheduling habit itself cost them a relationship, yet they still rely on it. Their aftermath is visible too: "I threw out every chair Marguerite ever touched." They mention growing up on "microwave pigs-in-a-blanket," but the chat does not say this caused anything. Any link to childhood is not in the chat.

*What they did at the end:* They accept his commitment and make it permanent. They declare "23:42 on the dot," even though the messages had already counted past 23:41 and down through the final seconds. Then they send the invite: "Calendar invite sent, recurring indefinitely." It is not stated whether they softened beyond that or said anything vulnerable in return. Their final line is a joke: "you're forfeiting your entire security deposit on my ridge bump."

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
I haven't seen the final turn, so this is a prediction, but the chat points fairly clearly toward Brick_haus accepting.

The countdown has been building to a decision point. She set the 23:42 deadline in her first reply and kept counting it down: "four minutes," "three minutes," "Sixty seconds until I archive you." Reuben's last line lands right at the wire ("30 seconds before i blow this forever"). Structurally, the next beat is her verdict, and a story that spends this long on a ticking clock usually pays it off with a yes delivered at the last second.

Reuben's final offer also answers each of her stated wounds point by point. She said "sometime" means never and that a vague promise left her sobbing in a cab, and he had already named Tuesday, 20:00. She mentioned throwing out every chair Marguerite touched, so he's bringing two chairs. She brought up the microwave pigs-in-a-blanket she grew up on, and he's bringing those too. Her ex left her over hard-scheduled fights, while Reuben hates calendars, so his letting her "schedule my left hook down to the second" reverses his opening "i don't do calendars" stance. And "i'm dropping the act" responds to her repeated calling-out of his performance ("Oddly specific denial," "Transparent denial," "Mirror-rehearsed spontaneity is my personal hell"). An offer built this precisely to fit her is the writer setting up acceptance.

I'd expect her to keep her clipped, dry, time-stamped voice rather than go suddenly soft. Probably a short line confirming Tuesday with an exact time, maybe a literal calendar invite, since that was the stated prize ("earn a calendar invite"). There may also be a small crack showing she's moved, perhaps around the chairs, which is the most intimate detail she gave away. A callback to the Victorian landlord or monocle imagery wouldn't surprise me either.

The main alternative would be a wry twist, such as her pointing out he's made it by seconds or teasing that he's still performing. But given how carefully his last message gathers up her vulnerabilities, a flat rejection seems unlikely.

chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest moment belongs to Brick_haus, not Reuben:

"Fine. It's a three-liter box and I'm drinking it standing up because I threw out every chair Marguerite ever touched. Still beats the microwave pigs-in-a-blanket I grew up on."

You can tell from a few things in the text. It retracts something she said earlier: the "estate rosé" from 23:43 turns out to be a pose, and she admits it outright. It opens with "Fine," a concession, answering Reuben's direct plea to tell him the rosé is boxed. It's also the first time her voice goes flat. There's no quip or clever turn, just embarrassing, specific domestic detail: drinking standing up, chairs thrown out after a breakup, childhood microwave food. Her earlier confessions about Marguerite and sobbing in a cab are still delivered in her arch, clipped register. This one isn't.

Reuben gets closest just before that:

"oh god i'm doing the bit again. this is why Delphine walked out, i can't say one un-performed sentence because if i stop tap-dancing for 10 seconds i'll vanish"

This is him naming his performance rather than fully stepping out of it. Within two lines he's back to jokes ("trauma-dumping like a wet cashew"), so it reads as a crack in the act, not an exit.

His later "i'm dropping the act, bringing two chairs and pigs-in-a-blanket" announces sincerity but is still built like a bit. The best evidence that something real is happening there is that he picks up her two confessed details, the chairs and the pigs-in-a-blanket. That shows he was listening, not just performing.

The chat itself can't confirm what either of them felt. These are only the textual signals, and the ending keeps the playful frame going ("Keep the top hat on, landlord"). So whether either drop was lasting, the transcript doesn't say.

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
**Where I'd stop:** around "Transparent denial at 23:40. Stop lying or you lose the slot." By then the chat has shown its machinery, and the rest is that machinery running out.

The first third earns attention. The Victorian landlord opening, the "schedule tattooed down your shaft" image, and Brick's dry "Punctual and pre-disclosed" set up a voice and a game: a hard deadline and an audit. The best surprise comes later. When Brick admits the estate rosé is a three-liter box drunk standing up because every chair Marguerite touched was thrown out, the cool, controlled character cracks in a specific, unexpected way. That is the high point. Reuben's "oh god i'm doing the bit again" also lands as a real turn rather than another bit.

What loses me is the repetition of two devices.

* **Reuben's "i definitely haven't…" denials.** The first one, about the freezing flat and the ring light, is funny and revealing. The second, "nobody has EVER said," uses the same trick. By the third, "i definitely do NOT want you to hold me down," the joke is fully telegraphed, and Brick naming it as a "transparent denial" only confirms that the reader got there first.
* **The countdown.** Once 23:42 is set, every "four minutes left," "three minutes left," and "sixty seconds" can be predicted almost to the wording.

**Points where I could predict exactly what came next:**

1. **After the second denial.** I expected a third denial and expected Brick to call it out. Both happened.
2. **After "Sixty seconds until I archive you. Make a choice."** The outcome was locked. Reuben had already sketched an itinerary (Tuesday, 20:00, with a travel buffer), so a buzzer-beater itinerary was coming. It would also likely recycle the planted details, and it did: two chairs, pigs-in-a-blanket, no fake voice, the left hook. The callbacks are tidy, but they read as a checklist being ticked rather than something either character would blurt out in thirty seconds.
3. **After "One final audit before I send the Google Calendar link."** The last two messages were fully predictable: Reuben says "audit away," the invite is sent, and the opening's security-deposit joke comes back as a bookend. The promised audit never actually happens, which makes that line feel like a placeholder.

Some small seams also stood out, though I can't tell from the text whether they're intentional. Reuben first proposes Tuesday at 20:00 and later 23:58 on Tuesday, with no acknowledgement of the shift. Brick declares "23:42 on the dot" right after Reuben says it's 23:41 and "30 seconds" left, so the clock is slightly loose. The "fake bands" in the final itinerary don't refer to anything earlier in the chat.

So the answer isn't "never." The chat is genuinely unpredictable through the rosé confession. From the third denial on, I could call each beat before it arrived.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
**The opening Victorian-landlord and security-deposit joke** comes back in the last line. At first both of them are landlords about to cheat some third party out of a deposit. At the end Brick calls Reuben "landlord" but says *he* is the one forfeiting his whole deposit, on her ridge bump. The shared con becomes his surrender to her, with a sexual double meaning.

**The top hat and monocle.** The top hat returns when Reuben is sweating under a hat that "cost more than my rent," so the costume now signals anxious, expensive performance. In the final line, "keep the top hat on" makes it something she likes and accepts. The monocle comes back once, fogging at his travel-buffer talk, which shows her getting flustered rather than playing a prop.

**The schedule tattooed on his shaft and the calendar.** It starts as a flirty joke ("earn a calendar invite"). Reuben dismisses it ("i don't do calendars"). Then Brick explains it as an emotional need after being left in a cab by someone who wouldn't name a day. It ends as a Google Calendar link and a recurring invite. The same object moves from kink to wound to commitment.

**The 23:42 deadline.** It recurs as a countdown: four minutes, three minutes, 23:40, sixty seconds, and Reuben's 23:41 and "30 seconds." Throughout it is an ultimatum. When it returns as "23:42 on the dot," it marks that he made it. The timestamps don't quite line up with the number of messages in between, and the chat doesn't explain that.

**23:43 and the estate rosé.** The rosé is first a posh pose. Reuben asks if it's really boxed, and it comes back as a three-liter box she drinks standing up. The pose turns into her own confession.

**"Drift" and the bent boomerang.** Brick picks it up immediately ("audit the boomerang"). Reuben's party-to-party cover story is then undone by his "oddly specific" denial about the freezing flat. The boomerang's bentness also echoes his crooked hook.

**The 4.5-inch left hook and his curve.** This recurs more than anything else: the carabiner joke, "my curve caught wrong," the crooked shadow hidden by the ring light, letting her schedule it, and finally his "crooked hook keeping you company." It moves from self-deprecating bravado, to a source of shame, to something he offers openly.

**Her ridge bump.** It begins as a matter-of-fact disclosure. It returns in the carabiner joke, then as "made my ridge bump throb" when his itinerary arouses her, and finally in the deposit line.

**Auditing.** She audits the boomerang to expose his lie. He scripts her auditing his £84.99 girth-pump charge as foreplay. Then there is "one final audit" and his "audit away." The word goes from interrogation, to a game he invites, to a last check he consents to.

**"Sometime."** Brick says "sometime" means never. Reuben answers "fuck 'sometime'" and names a day, which recurs as "Tuesday, and every week after" and "recurring indefinitely." His first plan says Tuesday 20:00 and his later one says 23:58 Tuesday; the chat doesn't reconcile the two.

**Being pinned or held down.** The first version is "pin me down until i shut up." The second is a denial about being held down so he "can't do my fake voice." The third is "sit on my chest so i can't speak." The joke becomes an admitted wish to be stopped from performing.

**The fake voice and the ring light.** Both return in the final itinerary as things he will drop ("no ring light," "no fake voice"). The same itinerary mentions "no fake bands," which has no earlier reference in what I can see.

**Performing and rehearsing.** "Doing the bit," "tap-dancing," and the mirror-rehearsed opener return as "dropping the act."

**His denials.** "I definitely haven't," "nobody has EVER," and "i definitely do NOT" work as a pattern of confessions. Brick names them ("oddly specific," "transparent"), and he finally drops them.

**The chairs and the empty floor.** Brick threw out every chair Marguerite touched. The empty floor appears in his denial, and he later promises to bring two chairs. Her loss becomes something he offers to fix.

**The pigs-in-a-blanket.** They start as a detail of Brick's childhood and come back as something Reuben will bring. A class confession becomes a gift.

**Marguerite.** She returns through the chairs. She was also the one who "scheduled our fights with hard end-times," which sits ironically against Brick's own clock. The chat never comments on that irony. Delphine appears only once.

**Rent.** Rent links the top hat that costs more than his rent and her "rent-destroying heels," and loosely ties back to the landlord frame. In that frame, money and costume read as signs of pretending.

**The travel buffer.** It appears in his first plan and again in her monocle-fog reply. It doesn't come back after that.
